finding.claim: Caller identity is taken verbatim from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header with no verification in the app, so any direct caller can impersonate any user who holds grants on a file and delete or rename it. Exploitable if the app is reachable without a proxy that strips and re-sets this header.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, read at views.py:11 (g.user = request.headers.get(...)) in the before_request hook, which runs for every route.
finding.sink: Authorization decisions: views.py:17 ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") followed by del STORE[fid] at views.py:18; views.py:25 is_allowed(g.user, f, "write") followed by f["name"] = ... at views.py:27.

trace.note: Identity read from header; no signature, token, or session check.
g.user passed as the user argument to ensure_allowed.
Grant lookup: resource["grants"].get(user, []) and membership test for the action. An attacker who sets the header to a grant holder's name passes.
Protected operation (delete) runs after the check passes.
Same identity-to-grant pattern for rename, checking "write".

finding.guards_checked: Only the grant check in acl.py. No authentication, no signature or token verification, no header stripping, and no trusted-proxy configuration exists in the repository. The header name suggests an upstream proxy is meant to set it, but nothing in this code enforces that. Severity depends on deployment: high if the service is directly reachable, low if a proxy always overwrites the header.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:11 reads the identity straight from the request header with no signature, token, or session check. acl.py:5 is only a grant-membership lookup, not authentication. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts on failure, but it only sees the forged identity. views.py:17-18 and views.py:25-27 have no other gate.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: the header is read at views.py:11, passed as g.user into the grant checks at views.py:17 and views.py:25 (via acl.py:5 and 8-10), and the delete and rename run at views.py:18 and views.py:27. Any direct caller who knows a grant holder's username can set X-Session-User-Verified to that name and pass, so the finding holds whenever the app is reachable without a proxy that overwrites the header; that deployment fact is not in the repo, so severity depends on topology.

finding.claim: File existence is revealed before authorization. Unknown IDs raise an unhandled KeyError (500), while existing IDs the caller cannot access return 403, so the status codes let a caller enumerate valid file IDs.
finding.source: URL path parameter fid (views.py:14, :22), supplied by any HTTP client.
finding.sink: Information disclosure via response status: STORE[fid] lookup at views.py:16 and views.py:24 occurs before any authorization check.

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for unknown fid, before ensure_allowed runs.
For an existing fid without the grant, ensure_allowed calls abort(403) (acl.py:9-10).
Same lookup-before-check order in rename; the unknown-fid path yields a 500 rather than a 404.

finding.guards_checked: No try/except around the lookup and no 404 handler is defined. The rename route does check before returning 403 inline, but the lookup still precedes it. Low severity on its own, and it also affects the unauthenticated-enumeration path of F1.

verdict.guard_found: none. The STORE[fid] lookups at views.py:16 and views.py:24 run before any check and have no try/except or 404 handler. The only checks are ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts with 403) at views.py:17 and is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, returns a bool) at views.py:25, and both run after the lookup.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: views.py:16 and :24 index STORE before any check, so an unknown fid raises KeyError (Flask default 500), while an existing fid without a grant gets 403 from acl.py:10 (via views.py:17) or from views.py:26, so the status code reveals whether a file ID exists. Any caller who can reach these routes can exploit this, and it is a real but low-severity existence oracle.

finding.claim: Conditional: is_allowed uses the Python `in` operator on whatever value is stored in grants[user]. If that value is a string rather than a list, the check becomes a substring match, so a grant such as "rewrite" would satisfy "write". The repository does not show how grants are stored, so this is unconfirmed.
finding.source: The grants structure on the resource dict (acl.py:5), which is data-dependent and not built anywhere in this repo. Stored data is not attacker-controlled through the code shown.
finding.sink: Authorization decision in acl.py:5, used by views.py:17 and views.py:25.

trace.note: delete check gated by this result.
write check gated by this result.

finding.guards_checked: No type validation on grants values. Only a concern if grant values are strings in the real data store. Reported as low and conditional; it does not hold for list-valued grants.

verdict.guard_found: none. is_allowed (acl.py:5) does no type check on grants values. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) calls abort(403) when is_allowed is False, and views.py:17 and views.py:25 test the result. None of these guards would stop a substring match on string-valued grants.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: acl.py:5 applies `in` to `resource.get("grants", {}).get(user, [])`, and views.py:17 and views.py:25 gate on it. Whether the substring match is reachable depends on the type of grants values, and nothing in the repo populates `STORE` (views.py:6) or sets `grants`, so the data shape cannot be determined; a grant value is also not attacker-controlled through any route shown. The claim is therefore neither confirmed nor refuted from this code.
